The DPA dismissed numerous challenges to the admissibility of complaints facilitated by noyb. The DPA found that the mere fact that data subjects were noyb volunteers couldn't in and of itself show that there was no legitimate, direct and personal interest at hand.

A complainant asked his company in May 2021 for a copy of all his timesheets since he started work, and the company only offered on-site inspection. The Chamber found that the company ignored the requests for a copy and gave no justification for refusing electronic transmission. In this prima facie decision it found that the company could have breached Articles 15 and 12 GDPR. It ordered the company to comply with the access and copy request and gave it a warning for future requests. This is not a merits decision, and the company may ask for a merits review within 30 days.

The Romanian authority finished an investigation in December 2024 into a company that had notified a personal data breach. A ransomware attack had given access to its IT infrastructure. The company had not applied adequate technical and organisational measures and had not regularly tested and evaluated their effectiveness. A significant number of people had their names, addresses, emails and contact details exposed. It was fined RON 24,866 (about EUR 5,000) for breaching Article 32.
The DPA reprimanded an online broker for failing to adequately explain to a data subject the reasons for not complying with their erasure request, in violation of Article 12(4) GDPR.

The DPA held that the implementation of an optional facial-recognition system, used to efficiently manage access to a football stadium, violated the principle of data minimisation as there were less invasive alternatives and therefore issued a €200,000 fine.

Following several investigations completed in December 2024, the Romanian authority found that Vodafone Romania repeatedly failed to keep customer data confidential because staff or processors did not follow internal data-handling policies. Incidents included sending an invoice photo to a third party, not using BCC in group emails, sharing a screenshot via WhatsApp, and sending an invoice to the wrong person. The controller was fined RON 74,526 (about EUR 15,000) for breaching Article 32(4) with Article 32(1)(b) GDPR. The operator has paid the fine.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in December 2024 into DELIVERY SOLUTIONS S.A., which had notified a personal data breach. Valid login credentials to the web interface of an internal application were obtained fraudulently, letting unauthorised people view personal data. The authority found the controller had not taken sufficient technical and organisational security measures and fined it 9,954 lei (about EUR 2,000). It also ordered corrective measures: an updated password policy, an access log, and regular security audits.

A controller installed a CCTV hidden in wall clocks within the neonatal ward. A loss or theft of CCTV memory cards caused a data breach, affecting 190 individuals. For violations found, the DPA imposed on the controller a total fine of PLN 1,145,891 (approximately €262,500).

On 25 July 2024 an employee of the public employment service, by human error, attached an internal Excel file with clients' personal data to an email sent to 292 clients; the email keyword filter did not stop it. The breach affected about 29,636 people, including data on their work capacity level, which the decision treats as special-category data. The service reported it on 30 July 2024. Acting on its own initiative, the authority found breaches of Art. 5(1)(f), 24(1) and 32(1)(b) and (d) and fined the service EUR 9,000, 15% of the EUR 60,000 maximum that applies to it.

The Italian DPA received many complaints from people who got marketing calls from real estate agencies that said they got their data from Realmaps. An inspection in April 2024 showed Realmaps sold lists of property owners with phone numbers, built from list providers' data and land registry data, without checking consent or giving information notices. The DPA held Realmaps was an independent controller, not a mere intermediary, and found violations on legal basis, transparency, accountability, processor and authorised-person designation, security, records, DPIA and DPO. It banned processing on lists lacking valid consent, imposed corrective orders and a fine of EUR 100,000, and ordered publication.

The DPA fined a solar panel provider €42,000 for sending contractual documents to all participants of a solar neighbourhood project. In violation of the principle of data minimisation, these documents unnecessarily contained personal information of all participants.

A bank customer made a subject access request under Article 15 GDPR for all his personal data, including internal emails about his case. The bank first said all data had been provided, then refused to share internal emails citing Article 15(4) and bank secrecy, and later said no further personal data existed, which the Commissioner found contradictory. The Commissioner found breaches of Article 5(1)(a), the second half of Article 15(1) and Article 15(3). He issued a reprimand and ordered the bank to provide the processing information and access to the redacted internal emails within 20 days. No fine was imposed.

The Estonian Data Protection Inspectorate (AKI) fined Asper Biogene OÜ a total of EUR 85,000 in a misdemeanour decision with two offences. The fines follow a late-2023 attack on the company's system in which about 100,000 files containing people's personal data, including genetic and health data, were taken. EUR 80,000 concerns insufficient security measures for processing personal data, and EUR 5,000 concerns breach of the rules on the data protection officer (conflict of interest and appointing a suitable DPO). The press release says the decision is not yet in force and can be challenged ("Otsus ei ole veel jõustunud ning seda saab vaidlustada").

Two customers complained that a payment sent to one of them through the bank's i-bank Pay app was credited to the other, unrelated customer, and that the bank did not answer their access requests. An on-site audit by the Authority showed a software error during the June 2020 integration of IRIS pay into Mobile Banking, which activated phone numbers that had never been verified by OTP. The bank then notified a personal data breach. It found 24 further affected customers and 38 erroneous transfers totalling EUR 2,149.66. The Authority fined the bank EUR 100,000 for the breaches of Articles 5(1)(d) and (f) with 32, and of Articles 25, 33 and 34, and EUR 20,000 for the breach of the Article 15 access right.

The Authority examined seven complaints against the National Bank of Greece about late or missing responses to data subjects' access requests, mostly for recordings of phone calls after fraud incidents. Replies came months late, and the bank blamed remote-working arrangements and request volumes. For the first complainant, whose recordings were withheld while the bank used them in a court dispute, it fined the bank EUR 20,000 under Article 15. For the other six complaints it issued a reprimand under Articles 12(3)-(4) and 15. In its own-initiative audit it found that the bank had no adequate procedures for handling access requests (Articles 12(2) and 25(1)) and fined it EUR 200,000.

The DPA reprimanded an employer for unlawfully processing allegations regarding the assault of a minor by an employee in the context of a disciplinary action. The controller was ordered to implement appropriate measures to ensure future GDPR compliance.

A borrower complained that the loan-claims management company had not properly answered his access request for his personal data and for recordings of his calls with its staff. The company asked him to collect the recordings in person, although it knew he lived abroad and had asked for them electronically. The Authority found that the contract copy was supplied late and that the call recordings were supplied only after the hearing. It fined the company EUR 1,000 and EUR 2,000 for these two failures. It also found the company's internal policy on access to call recordings breached Article 12(2) GDPR and ordered it to amend the policy within 30 days.

The CNPD's restricted formation concluded an investigation into an anonymised controller (Société A) over how it handled data subject requests. It found that the controller failed to answer 47 requests within the deadlines in Article 12(3) and (4) GDPR, and counted this as 46 breaches. It issued a reprimand and an administrative fine of EUR 175,000. The fine was calculated using the EDPB's 2023 fine calculation guidelines. The authority treated the breach as being of low gravity, but still considered a fine necessary to deter other controllers and to keep sanctioning consistent. The investigation head had proposed a fine of EUR 493,560.

The DPA fined a bank €50,000 after its processor unlawfully disclosed personal data of its customer to an impersonator even though the impersonator could not correctly answer identity verification questions.

The German Federal Data Protection Commissioner imposed two fines totalling EUR 45 million on Vodafone GmbH. Malicious employees at partner agencies that sell contracts for Vodafone had caused fraud, such as fake contracts or contract changes at customers' expense. A EUR 15 million fine was imposed because Vodafone did not check and supervise its partner agencies sufficiently (Art. 28(1) first sentence GDPR). A further EUR 30 million fine was imposed for security weaknesses in the authentication process when the MeinVodafone online portal was used together with the hotline, which allowed unauthorised third parties to retrieve eSIM profiles. Vodafone was also reprimanded under Art. 32(1) GDPR for weaknesses in certain sales systems. The fines were accepted and have already been paid in full.

This is the 15th annual report of the Bavarian DPA, covering 2025. Chapter 16.1, on the central fines office, mentions as an example a care worker in a senior care home. During his shift he streamed live on TikTok from the nurses' station and named residents and colleagues. The report says the fine office fined publication of sensitive personal data on the internet, but it gives no amount for this case. It says only that fines in 2025 ranged from two digits for a private person to the mid five-figure range for a company.

The Bavarian authority's 2025 annual report, in the chapter on its central fines office, says that, once again, a public 'wanted' appeal by the operator of a 24/7 automated shop was sanctioned. The operator had published images from video surveillance, hoping to identify two people suspected of theft and property damage. The report gives no amount, article, date or reference for this fine. It only says that the fines in the reporting period ranged from two digits (a private person) to the mid five-figure range (a company).

The annual report of the Bavarian data protection authority for 2025 describes several fines from its central fining office. In one case a sole trader hid an Apple AirTag twice in a company car to track an employee. She argued tax reasons and theft prevention, but the authority found secret tracking neither suitable nor necessary and fined her. Because of her economic situation the fine was in the upper four-figure range. The report gives no exact amount, date or case number.

In its 2025 annual report the Bavarian authority describes a security company hired by a woman for personal protection against her ex-partner. After a few days of observation, staff fitted a GPS tracker to the ex-partner's car, although no concrete danger had been found. The authority held the tracker unnecessary because milder means existed, such as continued observation or accompanying the client. It imposed a fine in the mid four-figure range, and the company's economic situation largely determined the amount. The report gives no exact amount, date or articles for this case.

A social services office employee was prompted by a social network app to post a photo of her current activity. Letters showing a benefit recipient's full name, household membership, type and amount of benefit and care-home residence were open on her monitors, and the photo made them available to others on the network. The authority found there was no legal basis for this disclosure of personal data, including health-related data, which breached Articles 6 and 9 GDPR. It fined the employee an amount in the mid three-figure range, taking into account the sensitivity of the data and the number of people who could see the photo. Her confession and remorse counted in her favour, and she accepted the fine.

Following an anonymous complaint about video surveillance at a campsite, the Brandenburg authority questioned the operating company, which cooperated only after repeated requests and only in fragments. An unannounced site inspection showed that cameras covered staff workplaces (reception, restaurant, kitchen), the entrances, dining and lounge areas, and guests' pitches, up into the awnings, without any legal basis under Art. 6(1) GDPR. The company's own statements showed that it had no data processing agreement with its external IT provider and kept no record of processing activities. The authority imposed three fines on the company, totalling an amount in the upper four-figure range, and the fine notice was not yet final when the report was written.

In its 2025 annual report, the Brandenburg data protection authority describes a case in which a police officer searched a police database for information on three neighbours and the building caretaker. He had told the caretaker he had run vehicle-owner queries on tenants and kept a folder with the information obtained. The officer had no official reason, and the report says he knew such access was only allowed for official purposes. The authority's fine office imposed four fines on the officer, each in the mid three-figure range. The report gives no exact amounts, and says the fine notice was not yet final.

For the 2021 federal election campaign, a district association of a political party obtained address records from the population register and used them to mail voters. The letters were made to look as if they came from well-known Berlin figures (testimonials), without naming the association as the controller or giving the mandatory data protection information. The association also passed the data to a service provider for printing and dispatch without a processing agreement. The Berlin authority imposed six fines totalling EUR 65,000, and the association lodged an objection (Einspruch). The authority counted the large number of affected people, the deception of data subjects and the disclosure of official data to an external provider against the association; its cooperation and the time that had passed counted in its favour.

The Berlin data protection authority's 2025 annual report describes a fine proceeding against an employee of a clinic who recorded film footage privately in the clinic and passed it on (an 'employee excess': misuse of data the person could reach through the job). The fine notice issued for it is now final. The report states no amount for this fine. The report adds that an employee's private misuse of data is not a breach by the employer, who must however report the incident without delay if the conditions of Art. 33(1) GDPR are met. The same section describes two other fines, on a doctor and on a receptionist, which have their own pages.

The Berlin data protection authority's annual report for 2025 describes, in a short passage on employee excesses in healthcare, a fine imposed on a doctor. The doctor looked up the health data of a female employee under his professional supervision in the hospital information system without any recognisable reason. He also checked the infection status of his assistant doctor without authority after a sick note. The report gives no amount, no date and no legal articles for this fine. It only gives overall statistics for 2025 (18 fine notices with 59 fines totalling EUR 79,450).

The Berlin data protection authority fined an unnamed medical company for failing to take appropriate technical and organisational security measures. The managing director's mailbox, used to communicate with patients and customers, was reachable through webmail for at least a month with only a username and password, without key-based or two-factor authentication. The account was then compromised and used to send phishing messages. The authority classed the breach as of medium gravity under Art. 32(1)(b) GDPR. The report does not state the amount of this fine.

In its 2025 activity report, the BfDI describes a case against a telecom provider that, in the BfDI's view, did not answer or only incompletely answered citizens' requests about their data subject rights in many cases. After many complaints, the BfDI opened investigations and issued instructions, some already final, and fined the company for 22 of the violations found. The fines ranged from EUR 7,500 to 20,000 and totalled EUR 177,500. The report names Art. 15(1) GDPR (right of access) when it describes what the answers lacked; it does not say which article each of the 22 fines was for. The company objected. The BfDI considered the objection unfounded and passed the case to the public prosecutor for court proceedings; the court has not yet decided.

The annual report describes a fine against a car dealership in Baden-Württemberg. Copies of ID cards and driving licences, plus test-drive contracts, were thrown into ordinary paper waste and fell from a disposal lorry onto the road. The authority found the dealership had negligently breached the integrity and confidentiality principle, and that a single central data-waste container was not enough for a large company. Because the company followed the authority's reasoning and cooperated, the fine was reduced and set at EUR 120,000.

A company in the cruise and tourism sector received an objection to advertising from a complainant under Art. 21(2) GDPR. It did not tell the complainant within one month what it had done about the objection, as Art. 12(3) GDPR requires, and the authority fined it EUR 5,000 for that. In the same proceedings the company contacted over 5,000 other people who had objected to advertising, because of a technical fault in its customer data. That breached the ban on direct-marketing processing in Art. 21(3) GDPR and drew a separate fine of EUR 70,000. The fine decision is final.

In the Hessian data protection commissioner's 2025 report, a cruise and tourism company ignored a complainant's objection to advertising and did not tell him within a month what it had done. A technical error in customer data maintenance also led it to send advertising to more than 5,000 further people who had already objected. The authority fined the company EUR 5,000 for the missing reply and EUR 70,000 for breaching the ban on direct-marketing processing after an objection. The fine notice is final.

The 2025 annual report of the Hessian data protection commissioner describes a case in which several police officers were involved. A man held in a custody cell was filmed by a fixed surveillance camera while performing sexual acts, and the live image was shown on a control monitor. Three officers photographed the screen with their smartphones, and one photo was forwarded and shared in a WhatsApp group, where at least nine people could see it. The commissioner found breaches of purpose limitation and lawfulness (processing of special-category data) and imposed fines of between EUR 800 and EUR 1,500. The report gives no single amount and no date or case number for this case; 17 fines in total were imposed on police officers in 2025.

The Hessian commissioner dealt with a company that, among other things, runs an internet platform for comparing medical and dental services. A complaint about an Art. 15 access request led to an inquiry, in which the company answered late, unclearly and incompletely. It did not use a three-month extension it had been given, and supplied the information only after being warned of a possible breach of the duty to cooperate. After the company made a few changes to its data collection forms, the commissioner closed the supervisory case. He then fined the company EUR 5,000 for breaching the duty to cooperate under Art. 31 GDPR, even though the complaint itself was largely unsuccessful.

The Hessian authority fined a company that offers apps and an online ordering service for restaurants. Customers' order history could be viewed by changing an identifier in the URL, and no technical protection measures were in place. The authority found a security breach under Art. 32(1) GDPR and an incomplete breach notification under Art. 33(2) GDPR. It imposed two fines of EUR 10,000 each, EUR 20,000 in total. The report says these were its first fines against processors, and that the fine notice is now final.

In its 2025 annual report the Hessian authority describes a fine on an IT company acting as a sub-processor for a laboratory operator. The laboratory ran an online service for retrieving Corona test results. A security flaw meant some results could be accessed without password protection, and some unauthorised accesses were detected. The authority had the flaw fixed and fined the company EUR 3,000 for breaching the integrity and confidentiality principle and the processor's security duties. The fine was set far at the low end of the range because the company was a micro-enterprise with low turnover and cooperated. Health data being affected counted against it.

In its 2025 annual report the Hessian data protection authority describes its first fine against a lawyer. A criminal defence lawyer posted a roughly 30-second video on his public Instagram account in which he leafed through an unredacted case file, so that data of at least 20 clients could be read. The authority found a breach of the lawfulness principle (Art. 5(1)(a) with Art. 6(1) and Art. 10 GDPR) and imposed a fine of EUR 4,000. It weighed the short duration, the number of people affected and the sensitivity of the data against the lawyer's lack of prior violations, admission, remorse and cooperation.

The report describes a data breach notified by a Hamburg hospital: two medical employees opened the electronic patient file of a colleague being treated there, although they were not involved in his treatment. The access was logged in the hospital information system. The Hamburg authority treated the employees themselves as controllers for this processing and fined both of them for processing health data without a legal basis. One accepted the fine; the other objected, and the Hamburg district court discontinued her case after two hearing days under § 47(2) OWiG. The authority says it cannot understand that decision and will keep examining fines against hospital staff in similar cases. The report gives no amount for these fines.

In its 2025 annual report, the Lower Saxony data protection authority says it concluded a fine proceeding against a credit institution over "Smart-Data" profiling for advertising. The bank built customer profiles from payment data, master data and data on the customers' residential surroundings, and relied on legitimate interest as its legal basis. After an attempt at a settlement failed, the authority fixed a fine of EUR 485,000. The report states that the decision is not yet final and that the presumption of innocence applies. The bank is not named in the report.

The Lower Saxony data protection authority's 2025 annual report lists, among its completed fine proceedings, a EUR 46,500 fine against a logistics company. The company monitored individual work areas of its employees. The report gives only this one-line description, with no legal reasoning, article, calculation or date for this case.

The 2025 annual report of the Lower Saxony data protection authority lists, as one of several example fines for video surveillance, a EUR 29,000 fine against a company that processed meat and monitored its employees. The report says that, to the authority's knowledge, no slaughtering took place at the site. It says the decision is not yet final and that the presumption of innocence applies. No company name, specific articles, date or fine calculation are given for this case.

The 2025 annual report of the Lower Saxony data protection commissioner lists, among its concluded fine proceedings, a EUR 14,200 fine on the owner of a pub. The fine covered the surveillance of employees and of customers, and also a breach of the duty to cooperate with the supervisory authority. The report does not say which article this fine was for; the duty to cooperate is Art. 31 GDPR, one of the articles the report lists as fined in 2025. The report gives only this short description. It does not name the person or the day of the decision, and it does not explain how the amount was set.

The Lower Saxony data protection authority's 2025 annual report lists, among its completed fine proceedings, a EUR 7,400 fine against the owner of a pub. The fine was for breaching the duty to cooperate with the supervisory authority, after several coercive penalty payments (Zwangsgelder) had already become final against the owner. The report does not say which article this fine was for; the duty to cooperate is Art. 31 GDPR, one of the articles the report lists as fined in 2025. The report gives no date, case number or further detail for this case. It is one short bullet in a list of examples.

The Saxon data protection commissioner's 2025 annual report describes eight fines in the private sector. One of them, EUR 7,500, was against a restaurant business that ran many video cameras covering the dining room, kitchen, outdoor seating and the neighbouring pedestrian passage, around the clock. Footage of guests, staff and passers-by was kept for at least 48 hours. The only justification was an abstract danger from the location near the border. The operator also gave no proper notice of the surveillance, carried out no data protection impact assessment, appointed no data protection officer and kept no record of processing activities. The report does not name the business or give a date for the decision.

The Saxon data protection authority's 2025 annual report describes a EUR 500 fine on a property management company. The company ran two cameras in a pedestrian passage that also led to a building entrance, and kept the recordings for up to seven days. The cameras filmed all passers-by and everyone entering or leaving the businesses in the building. The authority held this unlawful, because private bodies may not record passers-by on public paths. The fine was kept low because the company had already removed the cameras, deleted the recordings and cooperated during the earlier supervisory procedure.

A person complained that Google LLC, as operator of the Google search engine, had not properly satisfied his requests to delist links about a criminal prosecution that ended in his favour (right to be forgotten). Google delisted nearly all the links, so that part of the complaint became moot, but it unlawfully refused to delist one link (a reader comment under an article), which the Authority ordered removed. The Authority also found that Google's removal request form gave no option to attach documents (Art. 12(2)), that its automated COVID-19 'more time needed' reply did not meet Art. 12(3), and that it did not publish its DPO's contact details (Art. 37(7)). No fine was imposed; the Authority issued corrective orders.

The Croatian data protection agency, acting ex officio as part of a coordinated European DPO investigation, found that a Zagreb company had appointed as its data protection officer an employee who also held a general commercial power of attorney (prokura), creating a conflict of interest. It also found that the company had not published the DPO's contact details on its website at least until 22 December 2023. The agency fined the company EUR 12,000 and ordered payment within 15 days of the decision becoming final.

The Dutch DPA had fined Coolblue in a primary decision of 11 January 2024 for processing personal data through tracking cookies without valid consent, because its cookie banner assumed tacit consent and used pre-ticked boxes. In this decision on objection, the AP declared the objection well-founded and revoked the primary decision. It still found the infringement of Articles 5(1)(a) and 6(1) GDPR, covering 28 April to 17 June 2020, and imposed a new fine of EUR 40,000. The fine was set far below the category II starting point of EUR 310,000 because of the low seriousness of the infringement, the way the infringement was ended, unclear remedy period and the long time between the start of the procedure and the primary decision.

A man asked Línea Directa for a car insurance quote and was phoned by an agent of its processor, Majorel. Without his consent, the agent checked his driving licence points balance on the traffic authority (DGT) website, using an email address that was not his to obtain the access key. The AEPD found that Línea Directa had no legal basis for the points check, which was not necessary for the contract, and that its contractual arrangements with Majorel did not meet Article 28 GDPR. It fined the insurer EUR 100,000 for Article 6(1) and EUR 200,000 for Article 28, and ordered it to bring its processing and its processor contracts into line within three months.

During a rebuild of Panek SA's website, a subcontractor's employee mistakenly placed files with customer data from the old site on the new one, and Google indexed them, making them publicly accessible. About 21,453 customers and employees were affected. The Polish DPA found that Panek had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational measures based on a risk analysis, had not tested their effectiveness, and had not supervised the processor. It fined Panek PLN 1,527,855 and its processor ITCenter PLN 20,037.

The Spanish DPA investigated the professional football league LNFP (LaLiga) over a biometric (fingerprint) recognition system used to give season-ticket holders access to the 'animation stands' of first- and second-division stadiums. It found that the league, as controller, had not carried out a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) as required by Article 35 GDPR. It fined the league EUR 1,000,000, taking into account the league's arguments about audiovisual rights management and its turnover. It also ordered the league to suspend the biometric access system until a valid DPIA is carried out and passed, and to pass this suspension on to the affiliated clubs.
The DPA fined a business information publisher €40,000 and held that they erred in failing to regard information about sole proprietors as personal data and found numerous GDPR violations.

The French data protection authority (CNIL) sanctioned a real estate company for implementing unlawful employee monitoring tools, including the Time Doctor activity-monitoring software for teleworking staff and an in-office video surveillance system. The CNIL found breaches of Articles 5(1)(c), 6, 12, 13, 32, and 35 of the GDPR resulting from disproportionate worker surveillance, lack of legal basis and information, security deficiencies, and failure to conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA). Taking into account the gravity and intentional or negligent character of the violations alongside mitigating factors such as the company's cooperation and prompt deactivation of the software, the CNIL imposed a €40,000 fine. The decision was also ordered to be published on the CNIL and Légifrance websites without identifying the company by name.

After press reports, the Italian DPA opened an ex officio investigation into the municipality of Brescia. Fetuses and aborted products were buried at the Vantiniano cemetery with grave markers showing a first name 'XX' and a surname that often matched the woman's, and the same data could be searched on the municipal cemetery web portal labelled 'fetuses and stillborn'. This amounted to disclosure of health data without a valid legal basis and breached the principles of lawfulness, purpose limitation, minimisation and accuracy. The Garante declared the processing unlawful and fined the municipality EUR 10,000, taking account of the corrective measures already taken, and ordered it to confirm within 30 days that the portal shows only permitted data. The decision is to be published.

The Italian DPA inspected a credit-rehabilitation company after the Bank of Italy reported that its legal representative had made many credit-register access requests without proper authority. The inspection found no retention rules (data of tens of thousands of clients kept indefinitely in a single CRM), missing Article 28 contracts with processors, a data protection officer (DPO) who was not notified to the authority, and transparency and accountability failures. The company had named its own legal representative as its DPO; the Garante found that role incompatible with the legal representative's, so the appointment was void (Articles 37(6) and 38). The company also ignored the authority's request for information and filed no defence. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, ordered corrective measures within 90 days and imposed a fine of EUR 70,000, with publication of the decision.

The DPA has granted F.C. Copenhagen’s application to use facial recognition technology at football matches under national law since the intended enforcement of suspensions is a substantial public interest. No permission was given for non-football events.

An investor in real estate projects managed by the company complained that, when he asked for information about the projects, the company asked for a copy of his national ID without telling him how his data would be processed. After a sanction procedure, the AEPD found that the company breached Article 13 GDPR (failure to inform) and Article 32.1 GDPR (no appropriate security measures, since it asked for scanned ID by email). It imposed two fines of EUR 50,000 each and ordered the company to bring its processing into line within six months of the decision becoming final. The company did not answer the authority's information requests, and the AEPD rejected its proportionality and 'acting on behalf of a third party' arguments.

The Polish DPA opened an ex officio investigation into C. S.A., a company that profiles clients and prospective clients for credit scoring and credit risk. It found that the company's data protection officer did not report directly to top management and did not receive instructions independently (Art. 38(3)). It also found that the processing register omitted profiling (Art. 30(1)) and that no data protection impact assessment was made for profiling (Art. 35(1) and (7)). It imposed two fines totalling PLN 576,220 (EUR 132,000), and took the company's remediation before the decision into account as a mitigating factor. The decision is marked as not yet final.

The DPA ordered a doctor to rephrase their consent form as the purpose of promoting the doctor's services on social media was not clearly listed for the processing of data subjects’ pictures. Such processing without valid consent was deemed unlawful.

The DPA fined a company (controller) €10,000 for unsolicited communication, in violation of national Greek law, Article 11 (1) Act 3471/2006 (Protection of personal data & privacy in electronic communications).
The DPA found that Google LLC and Google Ireland Ltd. are joint controllers for the processing of personal data in connection with Google services in the EEA.

The Irish DPC announced two final decisions against Meta Platforms Ireland following own-volition inquiries into a 2018 breach in which attackers exploited Facebook user tokens, affecting about 29 million accounts globally (about 3 million in the EU/EEA). The DPC found infringements of Articles 33(3), 33(5), 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR, issued reprimands and ordered administrative fines totalling €251 million. The individual fines were €8 million, €3 million, €130 million and €110 million. No objections were raised to the draft decision under the Article 60 cooperation procedure.

A Finnish loan comparison service operated by Sambla Group Oy let borrowers' loan application data be reached through standard, shareable URLs, so third parties could see personal data, including national ID numbers, contact details and financial data. After a complaint, the authority imposed a temporary processing ban in March 2024 and then, by the Sanctions Board, a reprimand and an administrative fine of EUR 950,000 for breaches of GDPR Articles 5(1)(f), 25(1)-(2) and 32(1)-(2). The decision describes the infringement as lasting almost six years.

A Belgian hospital notified the DPA of a ransomware attack in 2021 that made systems, medical records and emergency care unavailable for days. After an inspection, the Litigation Chamber found failures in security measures, no data protection impact assessment, and breaches of integrity and confidentiality and accountability. It fined the hospital EUR 200,000 after reducing a starting amount for the hospital's financial difficulties, the COVID context and the energy crisis, and ordered compliance measures within 90 days. The Market Court on 3 September 2025 partly annulled the decision and cut the fine to EUR 50,000; the DPA has appealed in cassation.

The DPA reprimanded a gambling company for the improper design of their cookie banner. The graphical emphasis of the accept option and the additional steps required to refuse cookies made the consent under Article 6 GDPR invalid.
The DPA fined a newspaper €10,000 for failing to make use of anonymization techniques in order to minimise the personal data shown in a video that was part of an online article.
The EDPS issued a reprimand to the European Commission for unlawfully targeting X users based on their political views in order to promote a legislative proposal.

The ICO issued a reprimand to United Lincolnshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust after the Trust confirmed that between 1 March 2021 and 31 March 2022 it had failed to respond to 32% of subject access requests within the one-month statutory timeframe. The ICO found infringements of Articles 12(3), 15(1) and 15(3) UK GDPR, citing deficient SAR logging and backlog systems, inaccurate data supplied to the ICO, and a lack of oversight and resources. The Commissioner took into account the remedial steps the Trust had taken and imposed no fine.
A user repeatedly failed to unsubscribe from a newsletter despite confirmation from the controller. NAIH found the company violated Articles 6(1)(a), 12(3), and 25(1) GDPR.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in November 2024 into the Cluj-Napoca public transport company. Audio-video cameras in drivers' cabs on trolleybuses and buses, with remote online monitoring, processed employees' image and voice unlawfully over several years. The footage was also used for other purposes, including disciplinary proceedings against drivers, and the audio could affect passengers. The company was fined RON 19,902 (about EUR 4,000) and ordered to reassess the necessity of the cameras and the audio function.
The DPA issued a warning to a media company after it failed to adequately answer to and comply with an erasure request for more than a year, thus violating Article 12 GDPR and Article 17 GDPR
The DPA fined a controller €2,000 for sending nude pictures he had taken of the data subject to his own phone and storing them on it until the data subject noticed and demanded their erasure.

A patient complained that photos of her face, taken before and after an aesthetic surgery procedure, were published on a doctor's Instagram profile without her consent. The doctor said a former social media manager posted them and that consent forms lacked a publication clause; the photos had been removed and a civil settlement reached. The Garante found the dissemination of health data unlawful under Articles 5 and 9 GDPR and Article 2-septies(8) of the Code, rated the gravity as high, and fined the doctor EUR 20,000. No corrective measures were ordered because the photos were already deleted.

The Spanish DPA sanctioned CaixaBank over its online banking application, which let a representative of one co-holder of a joint account see the account's movements without the consent of the other co-holder. It found a breach of the confidentiality principle (Art. 5(1)(f) GDPR) with a fine of EUR 500,000, and a breach of data protection by design (Art. 25 GDPR) with a fine of EUR 3,000,000, totalling EUR 3,500,000. The proposed infringement of Art. 32 was archived. CaixaBank was also ordered to notify within nine months the technical and organisational measures adopted so that the online banking app protects all customers' data by design and by default.

Several citizens reported that the municipality of Portici used red-light cameras to detect traffic offences without any information signs near them. The Garante found that, from start-up until after its inquiry began, the municipality gave no first- or second-level information to data subjects and had not carried out a data protection impact assessment before starting the processing. The municipality had wrongly believed these steps were not required and fixed them once the inquiry started. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), 12, 13 and 35 GDPR and imposed a single fine of EUR 6,000, with publication of the order.

A former employee of the municipality of Corte Franca complained that a council resolution recording his resignation, qualification, office, hours worked and last working day had been published online and was findable through search engines. The Garante found there was no legal basis for this dissemination, contrary to Articles 5 and 6 GDPR and Article 2-ter of the Italian Code. The municipality had also communicated its DPO's contact details to the authority late, breaching Article 37(7). For the dissemination the Garante imposed a fine of EUR 6,000. For the late DPO communication it only issued a reprimand, treating it as a minor violation by a small municipality. The decision is to be published on the Garante's website.

A man complained that he kept receiving promotional emails and SMS from the website docenti.it, run by Start To Fly S.r.l., for years despite repeatedly unsubscribing and asking to be deleted. The company said it was an error caused by re-uploading an old mailing list and invoked legitimate interest and the soft-spam exception. The Garante rejected this: the only legal basis for such messages is consent, which had been withdrawn, and the deletion request was ignored. It found violations of Articles 6(1)(a) and 17 GDPR and Article 130(2) of the Code, banned promotional processing without documented consent, and fined the company EUR 10,000.

The Italian DPA joined three proceedings against telecom operator Wind Tre: an ex officio telemarketing inspection, a complaint about promotional messages sent without consent, and a complaint about a data breach. It found that Wind Tre could not prove valid consent for calls to partners' cold lists and did not adequately supervise its partners. It also found that promotional processing lacked a legal basis, that account access security was inadequate, and that the breach was not notified to the DPA. Because all violations had been remedied, it imposed no corrective measures but ordered a fine of EUR 347,520, about 0.2% of the maximum, and ordered publication.

A tenant complained about extensive camera surveillance in a residential building in Malmö run by the landlord company and about missing information. IMY found that the company had no legal basis for the surveillance (Article 6(1)) apart from the garage, and that its signs lacked the controller's identity and contact details (Article 13). IMY imposed an administrative fine of SEK 200,000, treating the infringements as low severity and negligent, and ordered the company to stop surveillance of all places except the garage and to add identity and contact details to the signs within four weeks of the decision becoming final.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in October 2024 into SYNOBIS MEDICAL S.R.L., started after a complaint about its website. The site placed cookies without prior express consent or information to users, and did not give data subjects complete information as required by Articles 12-14 GDPR. The authority fined the company 10,000 lei, issued a warning, and ordered it to obtain consent before installing cookies and to provide full, clear information on the website, mainly in Romanian.

The AEPD found that Generali España, an insurer, committed four infringements linked to a security breach in its SMC application: breach of confidentiality (Art. 5(1)(f)), inadequate security measures (Art. 32), lack of data protection by design (Art. 25) and failure to carry out a data protection impact assessment (Art. 35). The initial proposed fines totalled EUR 5,000,000. Generali paid voluntarily before the resolution proposal, without admitting liability, obtaining a 20% reduction to EUR 4,000,000, which ended the procedure. The AEPD still answered Generali's allegations (including non bis in idem and proportionality) and ordered it to carry out an impact assessment within three months.
The DPA fined a controller €20,000 for failing to respond to the data subject’s multiple requests to discontinue the delivery of advertising emails.

KASPR runs a Chrome extension that shows professional phone numbers and emails of people whose LinkedIn profiles users visit, drawing on a database of about 160 million contacts. Following several complaints, the CNIL inspected the company in July 2022. The restricted committee found breaches of the lawful basis requirement (Art. 6), storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)), transparency (Arts. 12 and 14) and the right of access (Art. 15). In particular, it found that contacts who had limited the visibility of their details on LinkedIn were collected through synchronisation of users' accounts. It imposed a EUR 240,000 fine, a compliance injunction with a EUR 10,000 per day penalty after six months, and publication of the decision, anonymised after two years.

The ICO issued a £120,000 penalty to Money Bubble Ltd, having determined MBL made unsolicited calls for the purposes of marketing and contravened section SSA of the Data Protection Act and regulations 21 and 24 of the PECR.

A Spanish financial institution was fined €500,000 for failing to ensure the confidentiality and security of customer data under Article 5.1(f) GDPR. A cyberattack exposed sensitive data due to inadequate security measures, violating Article 32 GDPR.

The Belgian DPA imposed a fine of 5 000 € for failing to uphold the right to object of a data subject by irregularly processing personal data and failing its obligation of ensuring data protection measures by default and design.

The DPA reprimanded a tech company for the centralised storage and disclosure of end-customers’ data to different retail companies. This practice violated the principles of data minimization, storage limitation, accountability, as well as data protection by default and by design.

A data subject complained that a vehicle history check company did not disclose the source of her personal data, did not prove its data was accurate, and refused to correct it. In an earlier decision of 16 July 2024, the Inspectorate upheld the complaint, issued a reprimand, and ordered the company to satisfy the complainant's request by a set date. This decision finds the company did not properly comply with that order and fines it EUR 12,000 for non-compliance with the order under Article 58(2)(c) GDPR.

The Region of Molise notified a personal data breach in its regional electronic health record portal: a logged-in patient manipulated a URL and could search and view data and health documents of other citizens (7 people affected). The Garante opened proceedings against the region and also against Molise Dati S.p.A., its processor responsible for technical implementation and security. It found that Molise Dati failed to put in place security measures appropriate to the risk, in breach of Article 32 GDPR. Considering the gravity low and noting its cooperation and quick remediation, it fined the company EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Molise Region notified the Garante of a data breach in its regional electronic health record portal: a logged-in patient changed a URL and reached a search function reserved for doctors, which let them view the health records of 7 other people. The Garante found that the Region, as controller, had breached the integrity and confidentiality principle, data protection by design and security obligations. It treated the gravity as low, noted the Region's high cooperation and quick fix, and imposed a fine of EUR 10,000. Publication of the order was also ordered.

The Molise Region notified a personal data breach in its regional electronic health record portal: a logged-in user with the patient role could manipulate a URL and search and view the data of other citizens, affecting 7 people. The flaw was a coding error by Engineering Ingegneria Informatica S.p.A., which designed and built the system as a further sub-processor. The Garante found that Engineering had not put in place adequate security measures and had not tested them properly, in breach of Article 32 GDPR. It fined the company EUR 10,000, treating the gravity as low and noting its high cooperation, and ordered publication of the decision.

The Italian DPA examined two complaints against the energy supplier E.ON Energia. One complainant received telemarketing calls based on a Facebook contact form she never filled in and got no answer to her access request; the other had her marketing consents recorded wrongly in the CRM and kept receiving promotional calls. The Garante found breaches of lawfulness and accountability, of the rules on authorising and supervising staff and processors, and of the rules on handling data subject rights. It fined E.ON EUR 892,738, banned further processing of the complainants' data, ordered updating of staff authorisation forms and ordered publication of the decision.

The Swedish DPA IMY examined Verisure Sverige AB, an alarm company, after media reports that employees had shared camera images from customers' homes. IMY found no proof that the reported image handling had happened. It did find that between 20 April 2022 and August 2022 Verisure kept access-log file names for too short a time to trace misuse, which breached Article 32(1) GDPR. Because the breach was minor and Verisure had already extended the retention period, IMY issued a reprimand and no fine.

A patient's anaesthesia questionnaire, containing another patient's name, PESEL number and health data, was handed to an unauthorised person. The hospital did not notify the Polish DPA within 72 hours and its notice to the affected patient lacked a description of the measures taken or proposed to remedy the breach. The President of UODO found violations of Articles 33(1) and 34(1)-(2) GDPR, fined the hospital PLN 29,684.04 (EUR 6,800) and ordered it to notify the affected person properly within 3 days. The fine was calculated under EDPB Guidelines 04/2022 with a low-seriousness starting point, adjusted for turnover and reduced for net mitigating factors.

The Dutch DPA fined Netflix International B.V. EUR 4,750,000 for not informing its customers clearly enough, both in its privacy statement and in replies to access requests. The gaps concerned purposes and legal bases, recipients, retention periods and international transfers. The case began with complaints filed by NOYB for two data subjects with the Austrian authority, which passed them to the AP. The AP treated this as two separate infringing acts, set the starting amount at EUR 2.5 million each, and found the seriousness low. It lowered the amount because Netflix cooperated, handled the complainants' requests, fixed the recipients part quickly and the case took very long.

The AEPD fined a cardboard packaging company for using a facial-recognition time-clock system for employees without carrying out a data protection impact assessment, and for failing to answer an employee's access request. It imposed EUR 200,000 for the missing impact assessment (Article 35) and EUR 20,000 for the access-right failure (Article 15), and ordered the company to fulfil the complainant's access request within 30 days. The company's arguments that the system dated from 2016, that the rules were not retroactive, and that the penalties were disproportionate were rejected. The access infringement was classified as very serious under Article 72.1.k LOPDGDD.

The DPA fined a university €40,000 for failing to implement adequate security measures and not notifying them in time of a data breach after a compromised email account resulted in an employee falling victim to financial fraud.

The CNPD's restricted formation decided on an investigation of company A, a Luxembourg retailer of telecom equipment, after on-site visits to three sites on 30 January 2023. The investigation concerned its video surveillance of employees and third parties such as customers and suppliers. The authority found infringements of Articles 6(1), 5(1)(a) with 13(1) and 13(2), 5(2) with 24(1), 5(1)(e) and 32(1) GDPR. It ordered the removal of two cameras lacking a legal basis and the deletion of their recordings, ordered compliance of the processing with the information duties, and imposed a fine of EUR 2,300.

The Authority examined a facial-geometry (biometric) entry system that the Vouliagmeni Nautical Club brought in at its entrance in spring 2022 for about 3,500 members and their companions. It acted on its own initiative after a question from a member's companion, and later received two complaints. It found that the club had not shown the system to be necessary and proportionate, so it breached the lawfulness principle (Article 5(1)(a)); having found that, it did not go on to examine a legal basis under Article 6 or an exception under Article 9(2). It also found that the club had not carried out a data protection impact assessment (Article 35) and had made its board president, who as the club's legal representative decides the purposes and means of the processing, its data protection officer, which it held breaches Article 38(3). It imposed three fines (EUR 28,000, EUR 14,000 and EUR 14,000), ordered an impact assessment and ordered the processing to stop until it is done.

After two online inspections of the orange.fr site and the Mail Orange email service in 2023, the CNIL restricted committee found that ORANGE SA breached Article L. 34-5 of the postal and electronic communications code, by displaying advertisements between emails without consent, and Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act, because cookies continued to be read after consent was withdrawn. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 50 million. It also ordered the company to make the withdrawal of consent effective, with a daily penalty of EUR 100,000 after three months. The decision is published, and the company will no longer be named after two years.

During ex officio checks, the Garante found that the municipality of Maddaloni had not communicated the contact details of its data protection officer to the Authority, although it had published them on its website. The municipality admitted the omission and communicated the details after proceedings were opened. The Garante found a breach of Article 37(7) GDPR and fined the municipality EUR 2,000, ordering publication of the decision. No corrective measures were adopted because the communication had been made.

During ex officio checks, the Italian DPA found that the municipality of Torre Annunziata had published its data protection officer's contact details but had not communicated them to the Authority. The municipality admitted the omission and filed the communication only after the proceedings were opened. The Garante found a breach of Article 37(7) GDPR, imposed no corrective measures because the communication had been made, and fined the municipality EUR 2,000. The decision is also to be published on the Garante's website.

The Italian DPA investigated Illumia, an energy supplier, after two complaints about promotional calls made on its behalf, one to a number registered in the Public Opposition Register. It found that calls were made without a valid legal basis and that Illumia did not properly select or supervise its sales agencies. It also found that Illumia lacked security measures against contracts being activated from unlawful contacts and against unauthorised access to its systems. The Garante fined Illumia EUR 678,897 (2.5% of the statutory maximum). It also issued a reprimand, banned further processing of the complainants' data and ordered corrective measures. The decision is to be published on the Garante's website.

The Italian DPA fined Foodinho, a Glovo group company, EUR 5 million for unlawfully processing the personal data of over 35,000 riders through its digital platform. The investigation found that account deactivation messages did not tell riders they could contest the decision, that automated systems (excellence score, order assignment) lacked human intervention and contestation safeguards, and that data including geolocation were sent to third parties without informing riders, even outside working hours. The Garante issued specific orders, banned further processing of biometric facial recognition data used for identity checks, and required changes to messages, GPS indicators and reputation mechanisms. This text is a press release, not the decision itself.

The Sanctions Board of the Finnish Data Protection Ombudsman's Office decided that Posti Jakelu Oy had no valid legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR when it automatically created electronic OmaPosti mailboxes for customers who were only signing up for other OmaPosti services. The Board imposed an administrative fine of EUR 2,400,000, together with an order under Article 58(2)(d) and a reprimand under Article 58(2)(b). The decision states that it is not yet final.
The DPA fined a County Council €29,500 for the excessive processing of CCTV footage of public and private areas and the failure to conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment.

The mother of a child under 14 complained that the father had posted a clear photo of their son on his personal Facebook profile without her consent. The Garante held that publishing a minor's photo on social media requires the consent of both parents, even under shared custody, and that the publication therefore had no legal basis. It found breaches of the principle of lawfulness, Article 6 and Article 8 GDPR, and Article 2-quinquies of the Italian Code. It ordered the father not to further process the image without both parents' consent (other than mere storage), issued a reprimand, and recorded the measures in the Authority's internal register. No fine was imposed.

A lawyer complained that the Enna provincial health authority published, on its website, a resolution approving its list of external lawyers together with an annex listing the 20 excluded applicants and the reasons for exclusion. The authority also did not respond to his erasure request and removed the list only after the Garante asked for information. The Garante found there was no legal basis for this dissemination, and that the erasure request was not answered. It fined the authority EUR 8,000 and ordered publication of the order on the Garante's website.

The Italian DPA checked the cookie banner and cookie policy of the e-commerce site aosom.it in April 2023, as part of a sample of online operators. It found that the banner lacked a free, specific and granular consent mechanism and that the cookie information was inadequate. The company said it had changed the banner; a later check by the Garante's office found that the banner's 'Impostazioni' button, though different from what the company had described, did give users those choices. The Garante declared the processing unlawful and issued a reprimand, without a fine, because of the specific nature of the check, the company's remediation and its cooperation.

The Italian DPA acted after the Guardia di Finanza's online checks, carried out on 5 May 2023, of a sole trader's website, one of a sample of possible e-commerce operators. The cookie banner offered only 'OK' and 'No grazie' and linked to a privacy notice that said nothing about cookies. During the proceedings the controller added a 'Gestisci preferenze' option, but the Authority found this only partly remedied the problems. The Garante found breaches of GDPR articles 4(11), 5, 7, 12, 13, 24 and 25 and of Article 122 of the Italian Privacy Code. It ordered the controller to bring its cookie processing into line, with a banner allowing specific and informed consent for non-technical cookies, and issued a reprimand. No fine was imposed.

A natural person complained to the Garante that Google LLC's search results, when searched by his name, still showed old news pages about a criminal case that ended with his acquittal. Google blocked most of the disputed URLs in Europe but refused to remove others. The Garante held that the remaining reports were dated, incomplete or not updated on how the case ended, which breached the accuracy and updating principle of Article 5(1)(d) GDPR. It ordered Google to delist those URLs within twenty days, without imposing a fine.

After an earlier decision (16/2022) fining the dating agency EUR 54,000, the authority received 15 new complaints about unsolicited marketing SMS sent without consent or any prior relationship. The authority traced the sending number and the website domain to the sole trader running the business. The controller never answered the authority's requests for views and did not attend the hearing. The authority found breaches of Article 11 of Law 3471/2006 and Article 31 GDPR, noted no compliance with the earlier decision, and imposed a fine of EUR 45,000. It also asked the telecoms regulator EETT to check the domain registration and consider deleting the domain name.
The DPA held that the erasure of all personal data from a former employee’s work phone by the employer was unlawful since it was not limited to corporate information.

The Hamburg DPA ran a sector-wide audit of major debt collection companies. On site it found that one company had kept a six-digit number of records with personal data after the retention periods had expired, in some cases up to five years, with no legal basis. The data was not passed to third parties in that time. The authority imposed a fine of EUR 900,000. The company admitted the violation and accepted the fine, and its cooperation was taken into account. A similar procedure against another audited company is still ongoing.

The Polish DPA opened ex officio proceedings after personal data of a company's customers was widely disclosed, and found failures by both the controller (A.) and its processor (X.). The controller was fined PLN 1,527,855 (EUR 350,000) for Articles 5(1)(f), 5(2), 25(1), 28(1) and 32. The processor X. was fined PLN 20,037 (EUR 4,590) for breaching Article 32(1) and (2), including in connection with Article 28(3)(c) and (f). For X. the DPA started from EUR 4,000,000, cut it to EUR 12,000 because of X.'s small turnover, then to EUR 10,200 for cooperation, and finally to EUR 4,590 on proportionality grounds.

The Danish Data Protection Agency reported the IT company Uptime-IT ApS, acting as processor for a chiropractic clinic, to the police in 2021 for inadequate security measures. A ransomware attack encrypted a server and the backups, and the encryption key had not been secured, so the clinic's personal data could not be restored. The agency also found that the processor had not set up or tested a procedure to check that backups could be restored. A court judgment of 12 November 2024 fined Uptime-IT ApS 40,000 DKK.

The DPA fined the operator of a website €350.000 (PLN 1,527,855) and its processor €4.590 (PLN 20,037) for data security violations after a configuration error on the website led to a data breach concerning 21,453 individuals

The DPA fined a postal service provider €200,000 for failing to implement measures which would have prevented thousands of letters being abandoned in fields and a river. Furthermore, the controller was ordered to implement a tracking system.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in October 2024 into Blackcab Systems SRL after a complaint from a customer. The customer had made an access request and asked for a copy of their personal data. The company could not show that it had answered the request. The authority found breaches of Articles 12(3) and 15(1) and (3) GDPR, fined the company RON 4,975.9 (about EUR 1,000), and ordered it to answer the access request and send the copy of the data.

A parent with parental responsibility for a minor asked a language tutorial centre, in May and December 2022, for tax invoices for the child's lessons and for information on the child's progress, but the request was not met. The Authority asked the centre for explanations several times and the centre did not answer the key questions, sending only a vague reply that it had sent the documents. After a hearing that the centre did not attend, the President, acting as single-member body, found a violation of the right of access (Article 15(1) with Article 12(1), (3) and (4)) and of the duty to cooperate with the supervisory authority (Article 31). A fine of EUR 1,000 was imposed for the access violation and EUR 2,000 for the cooperation violation.

The Italian Garante investigated OpenAI's ChatGPT service after a March 2023 bug showed some users other users' chat titles and some subscribers' payment data. It found breaches of the GDPR's lawfulness and accountability rules (no legal basis identified for training data), transparency and information duties, age verification, and the failure to notify the data breach to the authority. It ordered a fine of EUR 15,000,000 and a six-month public information campaign. The Rome Tribunal annulled the decision (judgment 4153/2026, published 18 March 2026).

Intesa Sanpaolo notified the Garante of a breach in which a bank employee accessed customers' banking data without a service reason. The bank judged the risk to be medium and decided not to inform the affected customers. After press reports in October 2024, the Garante found the breach carried a high risk, given its sensitive financial nature and the possible consequences, and that the bank had not shown a disproportionate effort. It ordered the bank to notify each affected data subject individually within 20 days and to report back within 30 days. It also recorded the breach and the measures in its internal register and ordered publication of the decision.

A former EYP employee complained that the National Intelligence Service sent lists with her name, university education and staff category to the Ministers and the Police Chief one day before the law on transferring staff to the Police entered into force. The Authority found there was no legal basis for the disclosure, that the lawfulness principle was breached, and that the controller had not shown it informed the data subject under Article 13. It fined EYP EUR 5,000 in total, EUR 4,000 for Article 5(1)(a) and EUR 1,000 for Article 13. It treated the breach as negligent, not intentional, and found no material damage.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation of Untold SRL in September 2024. It found that the controller never answered a data subject's access request and did not handle an erasure request within the legal time limits. It imposed two fines, EUR 10,000 for the access breach and EUR 5,000 for the erasure breach, and ordered the controller to answer the access request and to put in place measures and staff training so that data subject requests are handled correctly and on time.

The DPA ordered the public broadcaster to adjust its news website’s cookie banner since the graphic emphasis of the "accept all cookies" option invalidates the data subject’s consent Article 6(1)(a) GDPR.

Datatilsynet issued a reprimand (irettesettelse) to Disqus Inc. for sending personal data of users in Norway in real time to its parent company Zeta Global without a valid legal basis. The authority found that the consent relied on (browser default settings and consent terms under Norwegian e-communications rules) did not meet GDPR consent requirements, which breached Article 6(1) and the lawfulness principle in Article 5(1)(a). A fine of NOK 25 million had been announced in an earlier notice, but the authority chose a reprimand because the established breach was much narrower and the case had taken very long.

The Romanian authority concluded an investigation into Vodafone România in September 2024. A data subject complained that several email addresses, including their own, were disclosed when messages about a change of account manager were sent to business clients' representatives without hiding the recipients. The authority found Article 32 GDPR was breached because insufficient technical and organisational measures protected confidentiality. It fined the company 24,870.5 lei (about EUR 5,000) and ordered a reassessment of security measures, especially staff training and regular checks that instructions are followed.

A former employee complained that photos of her were used in brochures, mailings and training material by her former employer, a security company. The Dispute Chamber dismissed the complaint on policy grounds. The complainant had not shown she had exercised her erasure rights under Article 17 GDPR, and the file did not contain enough evidence to judge whether the processing was unlawful, since she appeared to have accepted longer use of the photos. No infringement was found and no fine or order was imposed.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation into Profi Rom Food in September 2024. It found the company sent copies of several employees' identity cards to a service provider without a legal basis, and fined it RON 49,744 (EUR 10,000) for breaching Articles 5(1)(a), 5(2) and 6(1). Separately, after a breach notification, an employee filmed a company monitor with a personal phone and the videos were shared on WhatsApp, which led to a warning under Article 32. Corrective measures were ordered on lawful processing, access to video recordings and regular staff training.

The Irish DPC investigated a complaint about LinkedIn's use of personal data for behavioural advertising and targeted advertising (BA & TA) and analytics. It found that LinkedIn relied on consent, legitimate interests and contractual necessity without a valid lawful basis for the processing concerned, and that its information on lawful bases breached the transparency articles 13(1)(c) and 14(1)(c). It imposed a reprimand, an order to bring processing into compliance, and three administrative fines totalling EUR 310 million.
The DPA fined a bank €180,000 for accessing the data of a former customer more than 47 times without any legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR after the contractual relationship had ended.

Grue municipality notified a personal data breach: documents about pupils' school-environment decisions (9A decisions), with names, birth dates, some national ID numbers and parents' contact details, were published on the public mail log for about three weeks, and eight further similar cases were found back to 2020. The cause was human error and weaknesses in the archive system. Datatilsynet found that the municipality had not implemented adequate technical and organisational measures for confidentiality, and had published personal data, including special categories, without a legal basis. It imposed an administrative fine of NOK 250,000, reduced from the NOK 400,000 announced in the notice after considering the municipality's size and poor finances.

A customer of an insurance company asked for a call recording and other customer-satisfaction survey material. The company first sent a written transcript of the call, and after the request was repeated it sent the recording on a memory stick. The deputy data protection ombudsman found that the company complied with Article 12(1) and Article 15(3) GDPR by providing the transcript first and the recording later, so no reprimand was given. The access right was considered fully met, so no order was issued.
“The DPA fined Raiffeisen Bank RON 99,466 (€20,000) after inadequate technical and organisational measures allowed for the misuse of customers’ accounts and personal data by the bank’s employees

The President of UODO learned from a private message that a public authority had no data protection officer. After requesting explanations, he found that no DPO had been formally designated from 25 May 2018 until March 2024, and that the DPO's contact details were not published or notified to the supervisory authority. He found infringements of Article 37(1)(a) and 37(7) GDPR, regarded as intentional, and fined the authority PLN 25,000. He also ordered it to publish the DPO's contact details within 7 days.

A former municipal employee complained that the municipality published on its online notice board several resolutions and determinations about his resignation, unused leave, a settlement and the appointment of a lawyer in his labour case, including a reference to a trade union representative. The Garante found no legal basis requiring this publication, rejected the municipality's transparency-law arguments, and noted the publication went beyond the 15-day period and indirectly revealed union membership. It found breaches of Articles 5, 6 and 9 GDPR and Article 2-ter of the Code, ordered limitation of the ongoing processing and fined the municipality EUR 8,000. The order is to be published on the Garante's website.

A debtor complained that debt-collection company Serfin 97 S.r.l. used an email address belonging to an acquaintance to chase a debt. Serfin was acting as processor (sub-servicer) for the securitisation vehicle P.E.S. S.r.l. The Garante found that Serfin had added contact data on its own without recording the source or passing it to the controller, breaching the processor obligations of Article 28(3)(a), (e) and (h). Because Serfin had already deleted the address and adopted new technical and organisational measures, no corrective measures were ordered, but a fine of EUR 60,000 was imposed and the decision is to be published.

The Garante checked the e-commerce website www.onlinestore.it through the Guardia di Finanza in April 2023 as part of a cookie compliance sweep. The cookie banner had no reject option, profiling and advertising cookies were pre-selected, and 22 cookies were installed whether or not the optional ones were accepted. The company did not contest the alleged violations and took the site offline promptly. The Garante found infringements of GDPR Articles 4(11), 5, 7, 12, 13, 24 and 25 and of Article 122 of the Italian Privacy Code. It issued a warning and a reprimand but imposed no fine.

The ICO issued a reprimand to Southend-on-Sea City Council, in Essex, after hidden data on a spreadsheet released as part of a freedom of information request revealed the sensitive personal details of staff, violating Article 5 GDPR.

The Danish Data Protection Agency opened an own-initiative investigation in March 2024 into the website boliglag.dk, run by Boliglag ApS. The site let users search property records by address or by a person's name, showing names, sex, age, sales history and sales value of current and former owners. The Agency found that this processing could not rely on legitimate interests under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR, because the privacy interests of the people concerned outweighed the transparency purpose. It expressed criticism (kritik) and took into account that Boliglag quickly removed the personal data from the site.

Following a complaint regarding personal data disclosure via its web application, the Romanian DPA (ANSPDCP) conducted an investigation into Your Consulting SRL. The DPA found that the controller failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures both at the time of determining the processing means and during processing, and failed to conduct regular testing and evaluation of their effectiveness. This deficiency resulted in unauthorized access between March and April 2024 to personal data, including full names, national personal numeric codes (CNP), vacation voucher information, and parental leave return dates. Consequently, the authority imposed a fine of RON 14,929.20 (the equivalent of EUR 3,000) for infringements of Articles 25(1), 32(1)(a), (b), (d), and 32(2) GDPR. In addition, the DPA ordered the controller under Article 58(2) GDPR to implement a mechanism for regular testing, assessment, and evaluation of security measures.

The Austrian DSB issued an administrative penalty decision against a COVID-testing laboratory company. From 19 May 2021 to 26 February 2024 the company had appointed its managing director as its data protection officer, without ensuring that his other role did not create a conflict of interest. The DSB found a breach of Art. 38(6) GDPR, negligence, and imposed a fine of EUR 5,000. A EUR 500 contribution to procedure costs was added, for a total of EUR 5,500. The decision is stated to be final.

The DPA dismissed a tenant’s complaint against the processing of their divorce status by their former landlord. The DPA held that the complaint was manifestly unfounded and excessive under Article 57(4) GDPR.

A complainant, represented by noyb, complained about the cookie banner on the RTL Belgium website. The Litigation Chamber held the complaint admissible and found that the banner had no 'refuse all' button at the first level and used an orange accept button against a background-coloured 'more information' button, so consent was not freely and unambiguously given. It found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and 6(1)(a) GDPR and Article 10/2 of the Belgian framework law, and dismissed the complaint about withdrawing consent. It ordered RTL to add a one-click refuse button at the same level and to use non-misleading colours within 45 days, backed by a penalty of EUR 20,000 per day per order. No administrative fine was imposed. The decision was later withdrawn on 24 March 2025 and replaced by decision 138/2025.

The Polish data protection authority opened ex officio proceedings after a personal data breach of 25 November 2019 in which unauthorised access to the IT infrastructure of a sole-trader business made customer and employee data unavailable. It found the controller had not carried out a risk analysis, had not regularly tested its security, had no ability to restore data quickly, had not verified its processor's guarantees and had sent defective notifications to data subjects. The processor, a civil-law partnership, failed to help the controller maintain adequate security. The authority imposed a fine of PLN 353,589 (about EUR 81,000) on the controller and PLN 9,822 (EUR 2,250) on the processor's partners, who are jointly liable. The fines were calculated under EDPB Guidelines 04/2022.
