A customer of VÍS, an Icelandic insurer, phoned the company with a general question without giving his name, and was later sent a service-satisfaction survey by email. He complained that the insurer had matched his phone number to its customer register and used his email address without a lawful basis. Persónuvernd found that VÍS could rely on legitimate interests under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR, given his customer relationship, the ordinary nature of the data, and the privacy policy's disclosure of survey use. The objection right was also respected because the email gave clear opt-out instructions, so the complaint was rejected.

The DPA fined a controller €5,000 for unlawfully publishing an employee’s image and personal data on the company’s website. Posing for a picture and providing data from a CV did not meet the consent requirements under Article 4(11) GDPR.

The DPA reprimanded an insurance company after it placed cookies without the data subject's consent and unlawfully transferred data to the USA through the use of Google Analytics in violation of Chapter V of the GDPR.

The Spanish DPA investigated Loro Parque, a theme park operator, after complaints about a fingerprint-based system used to verify entry with a multi-park 'Twin Ticket'. The company argued it only stored a mathematical representation and could not identify visitors. The AEPD held that this was biometric data processing prohibited under Article 9 GDPR without a valid exception. It fined the company EUR 250,000 and ordered it to stop the processing and prove compliance within 30 days.
The DPA fined a controller €200,000 for failing to ensure a level of security appropriate to the large-scale processing of sensitive medical data, therefore violating Article 32 GDPR.

The DPA fined a hotel €1,200 for breaching Article 5(1)(c) GDPR by retaining copies of travellers' IDs. The hotel was ordered to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, i.e. to remove the requirement to provide an ID and to delete IDs already on file.
The DPA fined an optician €20,000 for sending a former customer a marketing email even though she had expressly objected to this form of processing.

Datatilsynet opened an own-initiative inquiry in July 2022 into Dansk Retursystem's Pant app, which lets users receive deposit refunds by bank transfer. The app used a third-party account-information component (Tink) that could collect more bank data than needed, such as balances, loans and transaction history. The authority found that Dansk Retursystem breached the principles of lawfulness, fairness and transparency and data minimisation, and data protection by design. It issued a severe reprimand, an order to bring the app into compliance by 2 January 2025, and a warning that using such a third-party solution for this purpose is likely unlawful. No fine was imposed.

The Irish Data Protection Commission ran an own-volition inquiry into Meta Platforms Ireland Limited after user passwords were found stored and logged in plaintext. It found that Meta failed to notify a personal data breach under Article 33(1), failed to document breaches under Article 33(5), and failed to ensure security of processing under Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1). It issued a reprimand and three administrative fines totalling EUR 91 million (EUR 8 million, EUR 8 million and EUR 75 million).

An employee complained that her employer, a food company, never answered her access request for her Libro Unico del Lavoro extract and badge attendance records, sent by certified email in August 2022. The company said it was a human error because only the legal representative could read the PEC mailbox during the summer holidays. It supplied the data only after the Garante invited it to comply, more than thirteen months later. The Garante found breaches of Articles 12 and 15 GDPR and fined the company EUR 4,000. It dropped the alleged breach of Article 5(1)(a).

The Spanish DPA sanctioned Telefónica de España after an attack in September 2022 on an internet-facing application, during which massive requests (about 4 million a day against a normal 55,000) went undetected for days and affected personal data of over half a million customers. The AEPD found that Telefónica lacked adequate access controls (two-factor verification, blocking suspicious IPs) and alerting. It rejected Telefónica's arguments on legality, causation, culpability and proportionality. It imposed two fines, EUR 800,000 for breach of Art. 5(1)(f) and EUR 500,000 for breach of Art. 32, totalling EUR 1,300,000.

The ICO issued a penalty notice to the Police Service of Northern Ireland after a spreadsheet answering a freedom of information request, which contained hidden workforce data on police officers and staff, was published online on 8 August 2023. The ICO found that the PSNI infringed Articles 5(1)(f), 32(1) and 32(2) UK GDPR. It treated the three infringements as one penalty and put the figure at £5,600,000 under its Fining Guidance. It then cut this to £750,000 under its revised approach to public sector enforcement. The penalty is payable by 25 October 2024 and the PSNI may appeal to the First-tier Tribunal.

The CNIL restricted committee fined COSMOSPACE, a French company offering fortune-telling services by phone, chat and SMS, EUR 250,000. The case started from online and on-site inspections in November and December 2021, followed by a further inspection of the horoscope.fr site in April 2024. The company was found to have breached the GDPR principles of data minimisation and storage limitation, and the rules on processing sensitive data, through its shared prospecting database, and the French electronic-marketing rule (L.34-5 CPCE). The decision also orders publication of the decision, without naming the company after two years.

The CNIL restricted committee sanctioned TELEMAQUE, which runs fortune-telling websites and sends marketing SMS and emails from a database shared with COSMOSPACE. Following CNIL inspections in 2021 and 2022, the committee found breaches of GDPR Article 5(1)(e) and Article 9 (sensitive data) and of the French electronic communications code (L. 34-5, direct marketing). It imposed a fine of EUR 150,000 (EUR 100,000 for the GDPR breaches and EUR 50,000 for L. 34-5) and ordered publication of the decision, with the company's name to be removed after two years.

A data subject asked the Rome Prefecture (Ministry of the Interior) and a local health authority in February 2023 to erase data about a 2009 licence withdrawal for drink-driving, after the related offence had become time-barred. The Ministry gave no reply until July 2023, after the Garante started its inquiry. The Garante found a breach of Article 12(1), (3) and (4) GDPR, declared the conduct unlawful and issued a reprimand, with no fine, because the violation was considered minor.

The Garante received a report (not a formal complaint) that the website of Telerama News, published by T.A. Format S.r.l., did not display the privacy information required by Articles 13 and 14 GDPR. The company said that technical problems and a full site redesign had caused the omission, and that it had fixed the site. The Garante found on 15 May 2024 that the information was missing, held that the company breached the transparency principle and Articles 12(1), 12(2), 13 and 14 GDPR, and issued a reprimand. It considered the prompt fix and the absence of prior violations in deciding that a reprimand, rather than a fine, was proportionate.

A data subject registered on the Registro delle opposizioni (the Italian do-not-call register) received an unsolicited promotional call on 10 February 2023, made on behalf of a sole trader by a Tunisian call centre. The sole trader gave an incomplete reply to the data subject's access and objection requests and did not show consent, an adequate notice or a do-not-call check. The Garante found breaches of the principles of lawfulness and accountability, the basis of processing, transparency, and Articles 12, 15 and 21, and treated the case as a minor violation. It issued a reprimand and ordered a ban on further processing through external agencies unless compliance can be documented, an instruction to notify the call centre of the objection, and a 30-day deadline to report measures taken. No fine was imposed.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation at the energy supplier PPC Energie Muntenia S.A. in September 2024. A complainant had asked for erasure of his personal data and received no answer within the legal deadline; the reply came only after the deadline expired. The authority found a breach of Article 12(3) GDPR in connection with Article 17 and fined the controller RON 9,947.6 (about EUR 2,000). It also ordered the controller to handle data subject requests within the legal deadlines, including through periodic testing of the dedicated applications.

A complainant said the Ministry of Citizen Protection never answered his request about the lawfulness of processing for the new Greek identity cards. The Authority opened its own examination of the processing, heard the Ministry and the Hellenic Police, and reviewed the data protection impact assessment they produced. It found that the controller breached the information duties of Articles 13 and 14 GDPR and the duty to carry out an impact assessment under Article 35(1) before starting the processing. It fined the Ministry EUR 50,000 for the first and EUR 100,000 for the second, and ordered it to document why data beyond what EU law requires are stored on the card chip and to adjust the processing within six months.
The DPA fined a controller €25,000 for the unlawful recording of its employees’ workspaces and for unlawfully making these recordings available online.
The DPA fined a large electricity and utilities company €100,000 for unlawfully processing data without a legal basis.

Following a personal data breach notification submitted by Constanța South Container Terminal SRL, the Romanian DPA (ANSPDCP) completed an investigation in August 2024. The authority found that an unauthorized third party accessed employees' personal data—including full names, dates of birth, home addresses, phone numbers, and personal emails—stored on an internet-facing file management platform that lacked adequate security measures. The controller failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure continuous confidentiality and security under Article 32 GDPR. Consequently, the ANSPDCP imposed a fine of RON 14,929.50 (equivalent to EUR 3,000) and ordered the company to review and update its security measures, particularly regarding external network access to its data servers.

A mobile subscriber asked the telecom operator for access to all data generated by use of their mobile line. The operator sent call records and location and cell-tower data, but only on paper by post, and refused part of the traffic data. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman found that the personal data was not provided in a commonly used electronic form as Article 15(3) GDPR requires, even though the request was made electronically. The authority issued a reprimand and ordered the operator to re-provide the data already supplied in electronic form, where still processed. It declined to rule on which data count as traffic data, a matter for the telecom regulator, and imposed no fine.
The DPA fined a controller €1,400 for not complying with an Article 15 GDPR access request and for failing to cooperate with the DPA, thus violating Article 31 GDPR.

The Romanian supervisory authority investigated a complaint that SC Class IT Outsourcing SRL did not answer a request to exercise the right to erasure. The company could not show that it had replied within 30 days, and it replied only after the authority intervened. The authority fined the company 4,976.7 lei (about EUR 1,000) for breaching Article 12(3) and Article 17 GDPR. It also ordered a corrective measure to adopt an internal procedure for handling data subject requests and to train staff.

Following a complaint, the Romanian data protection authority (ANSPDCP) investigated Vodafone România SA for failing to respond to a data subject's request to exercise their rights of access and erasure within the statutory 30-day period. The investigation established that the controller only provided a response after the supervisory authority intervened. Consequently, the ANSPDCP fined Vodafone România SA 14,930 lei (equivalent to EUR 3,000) for infringements of Articles 12(3), 15, and 17 GDPR. In addition, the authority imposed a corrective measure ordering the company to adopt an internal procedure for handling data subject requests under Articles 12-22 GDPR and to regularly train its staff.

The Croatian DPA announced 12 new administrative fines totalling EUR 270,700. The largest, EUR 190,000, went to a special hospital in the Rijeka area. Patients' radiology images were irrecoverably lost in July 2019 because no backups existed, and the hospital did not notify the authority within 72 hours. The hospital also had no processor contract, no proper retention periods or legal basis for recording call-centre calls, inadequate transparency information, and did not involve its DPO. The remaining fines concern hotels (cookies) and video surveillance notices.

This is a press release announcing 12 new administrative fines totalling EUR 270,700. Fino's EUR 35,700 matches only one part: nine fines on controllers, mostly shops, for not marking premises under video surveillance. The signs were missing, not visible by the time a person enters the recorded area, or lacked the required information. The legal basis is Article 27 of the national Act implementing the GDPR. The release gives no individual amounts, controller names or reference numbers for these nine cases.

A former employee complained that the company never answered his access request of 7 April 2022 for his payslips and other employment data. The company also ignored two requests for information from the Garante, so the Guardia di Finanza had to serve a further request. The Garante found that the company breached Articles 12(3) and 15 GDPR and Article 157 of the Italian Code. It ordered the company to answer the access request within 30 days and imposed a fine of EUR 5,000, and ordered publication of the decision.

Three neighbours complained that a private owner had mounted five CCTV cameras on an outside wall of his building, aimed at a lane where their secondary doors and windows open. The inspection found five cameras, three working; the owner said that, for technical reasons, only two worked. The Garante held that the cameras captured areas belonging to third parties, so the household exemption did not apply and there was no adequate legal basis. It ordered the owner to narrow the camera angle within 90 days and imposed a fine of EUR 400.

The Italian DPA investigated Sky Italia after 275 complaints, mostly about telemarketing, and a separate complaint about a promotional SMS from the NOW service. It found Sky called numbers registered in the Public Opposition Register, used contact data obtained from third parties without checking valid consent and information, and sent promotional SMS to NOW account holders without consent. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, banned further commercial processing without checks, ordered corrective procedures and fined Sky EUR 842,062. The decision is also published as an ancillary sanction.

A member of the Carabinieri complained that the nursing order of Udine, together with other regional nursing orders, researched his profession and employer online and sent a note about his and his wife's repeated access requests and complaints to his military command. The order also failed to give an information notice, had no joint-controller agreement and did not answer his access request. The Garante found the processing unlawful, noting that the order only answered the access request after the dispute was notified. It imposed a fine of EUR 8,000, taking account of the order's small size, and ordered publication of the decision.

The DPA ordered the National Police Board of Finland to erase the personal identifying characteristics regarding a person suspected in an offence, which had been taken and processed unnecessarily and in breach of EU law.
The DPA fined a company €50,000 for unlawfully disclosing personal data in a mediation report, thus violating Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32 GDPR.

The DPA fined a clothing retailer €20,000 for failing to demonstrate that the data subject had consented to commercial advertisements when providing their e-mail address in order to receive a digital receipt for a purchase.

A complaint was lodged with the Belgian DPA by a complainant through the organisation Noyb, alleging that a Google Analytics embed on the Roularta website (flair.be) tracked the complainant and sent data to the United States unlawfully. The Litigation Chamber dismissed the complaint without finding an infringement. It held that Noyb's use of the representation right under Article 80(1) GDPR was an abuse of rights, because it rested on a fictitious mandate and a pre-set project of model cases. The dismissal was based on Article 100 §1, 1° WOG.
The DPA ordered a controller to bring the websites’ cookie banners into compliance with the GDPR by adding the reject button within its first layer and changing the colours used.

An employee complained that his employer made him use a fingerprint-based time registration system without voluntary consent and without proper information on storage and retention. The Litigation Chamber found that the employer unlawfully processed biometric data and breached purpose limitation, data minimisation and transparency duties. It calculated the fine under the EDPB 04/2022 guidelines, starting from EUR 2 million, adjusting to EUR 160,000 for company size, then reducing to EUR 45,000 after mitigating factors. The complaints against the system supplier (second respondent) were dismissed.

The Norwegian Data Protection Authority fined Eidskog municipality NOK 250,000 for breaching the legal basis requirements of the GDPR. The municipality had for years published confidential information about a whistleblower in its public postal journal. It also gave two former colleagues access to the whistleblower's report without adequate redaction, disclosing health and financial information. The fine was first notified as NOK 500,000 and halved because of the long processing time. The municipality has until 25 September to appeal.
AEPD fined a children's party venue after it disseminated CCTV footage in social media as part of an intimidation and online criticism againts data subjects, in violation of Article 6(1) GDPR.

The CNIL restricted committee fined CEGEDIM SANTÉ EUR 800,000 for breaches of Article 5(1)(a) GDPR and Article 66 of the French Data Protection Act. The company, which had taken over the activities of its subsidiary CEGEDIM LOGICIELS MEDICAUX FRANCE, collected health data from patient files held in doctors' software through a doctors' observatory and passed it to clients for health studies. The committee rejected the company's arguments that the data was anonymous and that it was only a processor, and ordered publication of the decision with the company's name removed after two years. No injunction was issued because the company no longer handled the data flow.

The University of Agder notified Datatilsynet on 14 February 2024 of a personal data breach. Documents containing personal data, including national identity numbers, exam accommodation and health-related information, and a list of Ukrainian refugees, were stored in Microsoft Teams folders that all staff, and in one case students, could access without a work need. The university had no procedures or training for restricting access in Teams, and the exposure ran from 2018. Datatilsynet decided that the university must pay an administrative fine of NOK 150,000 for breaching the security and internal control requirements of GDPR Articles 32 and 24.

Two complaints were lodged, one in Germany and one in Poland, about business profiles on the controller's website nicelocal.com that the complainants did not want published. Both complainants asked for erasure, and the controller did not act within the one-month period. The controller later deleted the content only after the Cypriot authority intervened. The Commissioner issued a reprimand for the Article 12(3) infringement, a EUR 3,000 fine for failing to cooperate with the authority under Article 31, and an order to review the handling of data subject requests within two months.

A complainant alleged that a police officer at the Capital Region Police filmed CCTV footage from a monitoring system on his phone and shared it with others, and that police staff disclosed information about his movements to his employer. The authority found it unproven that the processing was automated or formed part of a filing system, and unproven that it fell within the scope of Law No. 75/2019 on police and criminal justice data processing. It noted that purely oral disclosure of information generally falls outside data protection law. The complaint was dismissed on that basis, with no fine or order.

The DPA fined an electricity provider €25,000 for the failure to comply with a data subject’s erasure and rectification requests and for continuously sending incorrect invoices to the data subject, thus violating Articles 5, 16 and 17 GDPR.
